text.title: Python Type Hints Core Rules
text.summary: 10 testable rules covering union syntax, PEP 695 generics, boundary annotation, strict-checker configuration, ignore-comment policy, structural typing, payload-vs-body type choice, Pydantic at the IO boundary, the ban on bare Any, and incremental adoption.

rule.statement: Use PEP 604 unions (`X | None`, `int | str`) and built-in generics (`list[T]`, `dict[K, V]`) exclusively in new code. Ban `Optional`, `List`, `Dict`, `Tuple` imports from `typing` via ruff rule UP007 (`pyupgrade`).
rule.rationale: Mixing `Optional[X]` and `X | None` in one repo triggers linter warnings and degrades readability. PEP 604 syntax is shorter and Python 3.10+ runtime-supported. Pick one and enforce it project-wide via auto-fix.

rule.statement: On Python 3.12+ declare generics with PEP 695 syntax (`def f[T](x: T) -> T`, `class Box[T]:`, `type Alias[T] = ...`). Do not introduce new module-level `TypeVar` declarations; keep existing ones only until the module is migrated.

rationale.source: PEP 695; internal — python-type-hints backend copy, merged 2026-08-15.

rule.rationale: PEP 695 attaches the type parameter to the definition that uses it, so scope is obvious and the module-level TypeVar — which reads as a shared global while actually being per-function — disappears. On <3.12 the old TypeVar form remains the only option, which is why this rule is version-gated.

rule.statement: Annotate boundary signatures first: HTTP handlers, queue consumers, DB models, library public exports. Internal helpers get arg + return annotations only; locals only when mypy complains. Type the boundary before the body.
rule.rationale: Boundaries are where bugs cross module ownership lines; that's where types pay off most. Annotating every local variable bloats diff without proportional bug-catch.

rule.statement: Run the checker in strict mode at the module/package boundary — `[tool.mypy] strict = true` or `[tool.pyright] typeCheckingMode = "strict"` — and grant relaxation only per-module, to named legacy modules, never globally. Pick one checker per repo; `checker` in the spec records which.

rationale.source: mypy / pyright configuration docs; internal — python-type-hints backend copy, merged 2026-08-15.

rule.rationale: Strict is what catches implicit Any, untyped defs and Optional misuse — the cheapest defect-detection layer available. A global relaxation silently disables it everywhere; a named per-module override keeps the exceptions visible and countable in review. See `templates/mypy.toml` and `templates/pyright.toml`.

rule.statement: Never write `# type: ignore` without a specific error code. Use `# type: ignore[attr-defined]` / `[arg-type]` / `[return-value]`. Enable `warn_unused_ignores = true` so stale ignores fail CI.
rule.rationale: Bare ignores mask future bugs silently. Specific codes document the reason and allow CI to surface ignores that no longer apply once the upstream issue is fixed.

rule.statement: For cross-package contracts use `typing.Protocol`. Use `ABC` only when you control all implementers AND need shared concrete methods. Add `@runtime_checkable` only when actually calling `isinstance(x, Proto)` at runtime.
rule.rationale: Protocol avoids ABC inheritance coupling — third-party types satisfy a Protocol structurally without inheriting from your package. `runtime_checkable` is opt-in because it makes `isinstance` walk the MRO, which is slow on hot paths.

rule.statement: `TypedDict` for cache payloads, queue messages, and internal dicts crossing module boundaries. `Pydantic` (v2) for HTTP request/response bodies and external-input validation. Never define both `TypedDict` and `Pydantic` for the same data shape — pick one per shape and use everywhere.
rule.rationale: TypedDict is zero-runtime-cost typing for already-validated data. Pydantic adds validation + serialization but costs CPU on every instantiation. Maintaining parallel definitions for the same shape doubles the maintenance and the two drift apart.

rule.statement: Every IO boundary — HTTP request/response bodies, queue messages, and rows read from an external store — is parsed through a Pydantic v2 `BaseModel` before the value reaches business code. Internal, already-validated data uses dataclasses or `TypedDict` instead; never run Pydantic validation inside a hot per-iteration loop.

rationale.source: Pydantic v2 docs; internal — python-type-hints backend copy, merged 2026-08-15.

rule.rationale: Pydantic parses, validates and types in one step, and the boundary is the highest-leverage place to do it: everything downstream can then be trusted and cheaply typed. The same call costs CPU on every instantiation, so pushing it inside a loop converts a validation win into a throughput loss — hence the dataclass carve-out. This rule refines `typeddict-vs-pydantic` from the choice of type to the placement of the validation.

rule.statement: Do not annotate with `Any` in new code. Use a concrete type, a `Protocol`, or `object` for a genuinely unknown shape and narrow explicitly. `Any` is a last resort and requires a justifying comment on the same line. Every public function is fully annotated — an unannotated public def is an implicit `Any` and fails strict.

rationale.source: mypy docs — dynamic typing; internal — python-type-hints backend copy, merged 2026-08-15.

rule.rationale: `Any` disables checking on every operation chained off the value, so one `Any` at the top of a call graph erases the guarantees of every typed function below it. `object` forces an explicit narrowing at the point of use, which is where the author actually knows the shape.

rule.statement: Never run `mypy --strict` repo-wide on an untyped codebase. Adopt file-by-file: enable strict on touched files only via `mypy --strict $(git diff --name-only --diff-filter=AM main -- '*.py')`. Fix one error class per pass (no-untyped-def → var-annotated → arg-type).
rule.rationale: Strict on day 1 produces 1000+ errors and freezes adoption. Incremental gating lets the team make continuous progress while never regressing typed files.
